title: Sacrifice and memorial (CCC 1362–1372)
hook: the one sacrifice of Christ made present, not repeated

segments.voice: Yesterday, the names of the Eucharist: thanksgiving, the breaking of bread, Holy Communion, Mass. Your line was one gift, many names. Which name stayed with you? Day one thousand ninety-eight.

Is the Mass a fresh sacrifice every time? It's a fair question, and it can be asked sincerely or as a challenge. At Mass, a priest takes bread and wine and says the words Jesus said at the Last Supper. If that's a sacrifice, is Christ being offered again and again? The Catechism's answer hangs on one small Greek word. It's in Jesus's command at the Last Supper, and it doesn't mean quite what English means by remember. Today's word is that one.
screen: `A FRESH SACRIFICE EVERY TIME?` → `THE WORDS OF THE LAST SUPPER.` → `ONE SMALL GREEK WORD.`

segments.voice: At the Last Supper, in Luke's Gospel, Jesus takes the bread, gives thanks, breaks it, and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "This is my body, which is given for you. Do this for a commemoration of me." Commemoration, or memorial. Behind it is the Greek anamnesis. The Catechism says that in Scripture a memorial isn't only recalling the past. It proclaims what God has done, and in the liturgy those events become, in a certain way, present and real. It points to Passover: each time Israel celebrates it, the Exodus is made present to the memory of believers, so that they shape their lives by it. So when the Church keeps the memorial of Christ's Passover, his death and resurrection, the Catechism says that event is made present. The one sacrifice Christ offered once for all on the cross stays present. And that's why the Eucharist is also a sacrifice. Not because something new happens to Christ, but because it makes present the sacrifice of the cross, is its memorial, and applies its fruit. The Catechism is careful here. Christ's sacrifice and the sacrifice of the Eucharist are one single sacrifice. The victim is one and the same: the same Christ who offered himself on the cross now offers, through the ministry of priests. Only the manner of offering is different: on the cross with blood, at the altar without. Then the Church joins in. The Catechism says the Eucharist is also the sacrifice of the Church: the Pope, the bishops and the whole people unite their praise, their sufferings and their work to his offering, and the saints in heaven join in it too. And it's offered for the dead too. So the answer to the hook is no. Not repeated. Present.
screen: `DO THIS FOR A COMMEMORATION OF ME.` · `A MEMORIAL MAKES PRESENT.` · `ONE SACRIFICE, TWO MANNERS.` · `THE WHOLE CHURCH JOINS IN.` · then, large: `PRESENT, NOT REPEATED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember his sacrifice at Mass. Start now, so you're ready when you're next there. Settle, and breathe. Picture the moment in the Mass when the priest repeats the words of the Last Supper and lifts up the host. Decide now what you'll bring to that moment: one worry, one piece of work, one person, one hard thing from this week. The Catechism says people can unite these to his offering. If you pray, you can hold that one thing now, ready to bring. If you don't go to Mass, simply hold it, and notice what it would mean to offer it. The bell holds the time.
Anamnesis. Memorial: not just remembering the past, but making Christ's one sacrifice present in the liturgy. Today's word.
Your line: present, not repeated. Today, take one thing you'd normally just remember about someone you love, and make it present: say it to them, or show it, today. Day one thousand ninety-eight.

howItsDone: At each Mass the priest repeats Christ's words over the bread and wine; the congregation is invited to offer their own lives with Christ's offering, and Masses are often offered for the dead.

fork.setup: a friend asks: if the Mass is a sacrifice, isn't Christ being offered again and again? how does the Catechism answer?
options: yes, a new sacrifice each time.
no, it's only a reminder, like a photo.
no, the one sacrifice of the cross is made present.
fork.reveal: the Eucharist makes present the one sacrifice of the cross, is its memorial, and applies its fruit: present, not repeated.

original.note: Greek: the memorial word in Jesus's command, do this for a commemoration of me.

trapdoor: what you thought: memorial means remembering something that's over.
what it means: a memorial that makes present: the one sacrifice of Christ, not repeated, present again at the altar.
what a scholar hears: Catechism 1367, from the Council of Trent: one and the same victim; only the manner of offering is different.

sources.quoted: This is my body, which is given for you. Do this for a commemoration of me.

sources.ref: Council of Trent, Session XXII, chapter 2

notes: That 'commemoration' renders Greek anamnesis in Luke 22:19 is a fact about the text; CCC 1362–1364 use 'memorial'. Confirm.
Trent (via CCC 1367) paraphrased; 'with blood / without' summarizes 'bloody / unbloody manner'.
Passover mentioned as CCC 1363 frames it, describing Israel's own understanding without comparison; Keeper should check tone.
howItsDone: 'Masses are often offered for the dead' (cf. CCC 1371) — confirm.
Original: ἀνάμνησις; confirm accent and pronunciation.
Editor pass: hook no longer claims how people ask the question; garbled Trent sentence ('who then offered himself') rewritten for clarity.

Audit pass: teach no longer has the saints in heaven offering their sufferings (CCC 1368 speaks of the faithful's sufferings; CCC 1370 of the saints joining the offering); carry no longer says 'do it again', which cut against 'not repeated'.
